General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Hikers Stuck in a Stampede & Catch a Miracle Hitch After Dark

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3198 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that this morning we packed up early at our tent site, knowing that within in a couple of hours we would be meeting our friend, Gorf, at a nearby trailhead.
  • The sun coming up as we made our way to the trailhead to meet up with Gorf.
  • Both of us planned to leave about 2-3 days of food with Gorf so that we wouldn’t have to carry a huge resupply for this section.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this morning we packed up early at our tent site, knowing that within in a couple of hours we would be meeting our friend, Gorf, at a nearby trailhead. We were only about 6 miles out from the trailhead from the spot that we camped at last night. Those 6 miles were actually some of the easiest that we’ve had out here on the Arizona Trail. There was hardly any elevation gain, and the trail wasn’t covered in any loose rocks. A lot of the miles of trail along the Arizona Trail have loose, rocky sections which can definitely slow me down. Being able to start our day on such nice terrain was delightful. Plus, we were both excited to see Gorf and get some food from her.

The sun coming up as we made our way to the trailhead to meet up with Gorf.

Both of us planned to leave about 2-3 days of food with Gorf so that we wouldn’t have to carry a huge resupply for this section. She offered to drive out and meet us somewhere and this wound up being the perfect opportunity. Of course, we weren’t expecting another big storm to roll in. But it all worked out, nevertheless. By around 8:15AM, Slide and I got to the trailhead and sat down to wait for Gorf. We couldn’t have been there for more than a minute or two when she drove up and parked in the pull off. It was really nice to see her again after having spent so much time with her and Slash on this trail so far. The day we spent hiking down into the Grand Canyon with Slash and Gorf was the only day so far that we actually hiked with anyone else out here.

I really liked the way these tall plants looked in the rising sun.

We hung out at the trailhead with Gorf for a little while. She had brought us both the resupplies that we left at her house but also brought us each a chocolate milk and a breakfast sandwich from McDonald’s. That was an incredible way to start off the day. I actually somehow packed the perfect amount of food for this section of trail. If this storm wasn’t coming and we were going to hike all day today and tomorrow, I would’ve nailed it! Even still, I only had a little bit of food left this morning before meeting Gorf. And the amount of food that I had left at her house wasn’t too crazy. Slide on the other hand had left an obscene amount of food at Gorf and Slash’s place! He definitely eats more than me, as he should, but also still had a good amount of food leftover last night and this morning. Watching him stuff his food bag into his backpack was hilarious, as it basically took up the space of his entire pack. I could not have carried that backpack around all day.

Recent findings suggest that unfortunately, we still had 28 miles to hike for the day, so we couldn’t stick around at the trailhead with Gorf for too long. We gave her a rundown on our initiative to get to the upcoming highway in 28 miles and hitch into Strawberry, AZ this evening. I did the math and it looked like we would be getting to the trailhead sometime after dark. So, this morning I was texting numbers off of the Arizona Trail Angels list to see about scheduling a ride into town this evening. But we were out of range for a lot of people, and a few people were out of town or otherwise unavailable. I had gotten one response from a couple who mentioned they could bring us into town first thing tomorrow morning, which was an excellent backup plan if all else failed. However, I wasn’t able to secure us a ride just yet. It looks like we’re just going to have to wing it this evening! Of course, Gorf is the absolutely sweetest human ever and offered to drive all the way back out here this evening to drive us into town. But we couldn’t possibly let her drive that far so late at night for that! She would get home so late after dropping us off. We told her that we would figure it out one way or another. The trail hardly ever fails you when you’re out thru hiking, so we’ll just have to hope for the best.

When we left that trailhead, we briefly continued through a wooded area before crossing over another dirt road and second trailhead. There was a trail register at this spot, so we stopped to sign it and shed some of our morning layers. The sun was rising and already starting to warm us up nicely. I’ve been loving the trail registers on this hike because there are actually a bunch of people ahead of us. It’s fun to see where everyone is and be able to get excited about catching up to some hikers. Our friends Woods, Strix, and Leaf signed this trail register this morning. They had remarked that they were trying to camp by the trailhead last night and were probably a couple of hours ahead of us. Everyone is just trying to get to that highway up ahead and go into town from there if possible. I texted Wood’s to see about joining forces and coordinating on a trail angel ride. But lucky for them, they actually might reach the road before it gets dark. I hope that they do and we can just figure out our own ride into town somehow.

Those next couple of hours after leaving the trailhead were nice and easy. The trail continued through pine forest which was occasionally adorned by small wildflowers. The time was passing by quickly and the trail was following along a wide-open prairie filled with cows. We could hear the moo-ing grow closer and closer as we continued on. Eventually the hoard of cows was all around us and I had the feeling that things were about to get interesting. I could see masses of cows all across the trail in front of me. It was like we were in the center of all of them! Then I heard the undeniable sound of a cowboy’s whistle, and I knew what was happening. They were herding all of the cows through this area, and we were smack dab in the center. We were able to continue on a bit further before a cowboy asked us to stop where we were so they could get the rest of the cows past us. Slide and I stood by a group of trees and watched as a few different men and women on horseback, and one dog, herded all of those cows right on by. That was honestly one of the coolest things that I’d ever been in the middle of! It felt like we were back in Montana, certainly not here in Arizona.

It has been revealed that the calm before the storm. There were hundreds of cows alongside the trail, but I certainly didn’t expect to encounter and massive group of them all around us.

With the enormous herd of cattle now behind us, we continued on through prairies and scarce pine forests. Those miles flew by and terrain was taking it easy on our feet for once. A few miles after our encounter with all of the cows we stumbled upon a massive group of antelope off in the distance. At first, it only appeared to be about 10-20 of them, but once we startled the group and they began to run off, we noticed just how many there were. It had to have been nearly 50 antelope all running by in the distance. I hadn’t seen anything like that since the CDT and really wasn’t expecting to see antelope out here. I guess that is one of the nice things about attempting a thru hike with minimal research prior to setting out. Everything out here winds up being a delightful surprise!

Tons of cows lining the forest up ahead of us.

According to recent reports, over the next handful of miles, the trail did get a bit rockier which wasn’t ideal. My body and especially my feet were tired from the big mile days back-to-back. I was definitely hoping that the miles would be as easy as they possibly could be. Regardless, we continued on just the same. And sometime around 3PM we passed by what would likely be our last water source for the day. There was a water cache right by the highway, but I was hoping that we wouldn’t be needing that! If we got a ride into town then we wouldn’t have to be cooking dinner tonight. This seemed like as good a place as any to stop off for a quick break and reset. We had been keeping our heads down as much as we could today and were making really great time. But it still wasn’t looking humanly possible for us to make it to the highway before the sun went down. Especially if the terrain was going to be even remotely muddy or rocky, which would just slow us down. There were still about 12 miles standing between us and the highway.

Recent findings suggest that this is what most of our day looked like. I’ve been loving the way the wheatgrass moved in the breeze alongside the trail.

When we set out from there saw that the trail was going to be crossing over a dirt road in about 5-6 miles. It looked like we could hop onto the road and walk it for a few miles toward the end of the day. Maybe that would help us buy some time and be able to make it to the road before dark? That was at least what I was hoping. For those next couple of hours, the two of us were hustling and trying to keep a good pace going. By the time we reached that dirt road crossing it was after 5PM and we still had a way to go. The sun was already starting to go down so we stopped off to put some layers on. I checked my phone and had a message from Wood’s saying that she had made it to the road crossing and managed to get a quick hitch into Strawberry. Strix and Leaf were still behind her somewhere and were also hoping to get a hitch before dark. I figured we might catch them along the way today but hadn’t caught up to them yet. Knowing that Wood’s had gotten a quick hitch definitely gave me hope. But hitch hiking in the dark is its own beast entirely.

It has been revealed that it was a relief to hop onto the dirt road and know that those miles would be quick and easy. We walked along it for nearly an hour and did have one ATV and one truck go by us, though they weren’t going in the direction that we were headed. Then the sun finally set and we put our headlamps on and continued on in the dark. At this point hope was dwindling, but I wasn’t ready to give up. I told Slide that we were going to get a magical hitch one way or another. Pretty soon we would be approaching the point where the trail crossed back over the road, and we would continue on the trail for a little less than 2 miles before reaching the highway. And just then, that same truck that had driven past us earlier was now driving back by us the other direction. The man inside rolled down the window and asked us the million-dollar question, “Do you guys need a ride?”. We were 2 miles shy of the highway crossing where we were planning to hitch into town, but those extra miles didn’t have to get hiked tonight! Yes, we did need a ride to town!

According to recent reports, the guys were out scouting the area for hunting and were heading all the way back to Payson. In order to get to Payson, you have to drive right through Strawberry, and then through Pine. When we told them where we were headed, they offered to drive us all the way there! Slide and I were stoked. I was trying to remain hopeful, but in my heart I knew how hard it was going to be for us to get a hitch after dark. And this one landed right in our laps. We got into the car and the guys continued down the dirt road until we were out at the highway. I mentioned that we would actually be driving right past the Arizona Trail trailhead and was pointing it out to the guys. They asked if there might be any other hikers there that we knew, and I responded that there definitely might be! If Strix and Leaf hadn’t gotten a ride yet, then they might be standing right there at the trail trying to hitch. When we drove by the guy who was driving couldn’t see anyone standing there but Slide and I saw the gleam of their red lights alongside the road. We told the driver that we saw our friends and he pulled over right away.

Slide and I in the back of the truck bed, riding to town in the dark.

According to recent reports, I think the best part about picking up the girls was seeing how surprised they were when the car pulled over and Slide and I got out of the truck. Strix screamed in excitement and we were just laughing, standing there along the road. There was only space for two people inside so we offered for the girls to warm up in the truck, and we could sit in bed. I’ve never ridden in the back of a pickup truck at night before! Once we got in the truck bed, I put my Sambob alpha layers on and my puffy jacket. It was going to be cold back there once the car was moving. But it was a beautiful night, and I didn’t mind it at all. The ride to Strawberry was about 25-30 minutes and we got to watch the stars and the view all from the back of the truck bed. That was pretty awesome.

Those guys drove us all the way to Strawberry and even went down the numerous side roads to get us to the Airbnb where all of the other hikers are staying. Then they dropped the four of us off and we headed inside to see our friends. When I opened the door, everyone gave a little cheer as us remaining stragglers arrived to beat the incoming storm. There on the couch was 9 Lives, Kitty Hawk, Lazarus, PI, Lizard, and Wood’s. We haven’t seen most of this group since the other hiker Airbnb back in Flagstaff. It was so awesome to get there and know that we didn’t have to deal with packing up in the rain tomorrow and trying to get a ride into town. The first thing 9 Lives did was come over and give me a big hug, then demonstrated me to the room that we would be able to stay in for the night. There were two sets of bunk beds each with full sized beds at the bottom. There were going to be 6 of us in that room tonight! But I was just so glad to be sleeping anywhere indoors tonight.

Recent findings suggest that once we dropped our things we hung out with everyone and joined them in watching a movie. They had made burgers for dinner and offered us some food which was wonderful. Then I took a long, hot shower and we even got things together to do laundry. Their Airbnb was this adorable cabin and apparently there have been a lot of elk in the yard the last couple of days. This group got into town 4 days ago and have been hanging out waiting out the storm. A couple people are dealing with some foot and ankle issues, so it just made more sense for them to all relax and wait out the weather, rather than pushing significant miles to get up ahead before the storm. I’m sure glad that they did, because now we are actually almost caught up to this group! When we all get back on trail in a couple of days, Slide and I will still be able 38 miles behind the big group. But we were 150+ miles behind before. That means we definitely stand a chance of catching up to everyone soon. And Strix, Woods, and Leaf all got off at the same road crossing as us. So, we’ll all get back on trail together in a couple days too.

A bunch of us wound up staying up and watching another movie after that first one ended. It was really nice to just sit there on the couch, surrounded by other hikers, and just relax. We’ve been pushing substantial miles for the past couple of days to get here. I’m looking forward to the rain coming and us having no other choice but to slow down and rest.

According to recent reports, I’m a thru hiker who has hiked 23,000+ miles in the last few years. In 2025 I became the 1st known woman to hike the “Border to Border” Calendar Year Triple Crown & complete over 10,000 miles of hiking in 1 year. In 2023 I became the 2nd known woman to hike the Eastern Continental Trail from Key West, Florida to Newfoundland Canada. I completed my Double Triple Crown between 2022-2025.

Recent findings suggest that strawberry/Pine… Spent many many weekends up there. My most favorite place. Beware of altitude sleepiness. Makes ya wanna nap like crazy! Lotsa elk & deer that are almost tame. You should see those massive elk stand up on their back legs to reach something to eat in a tree. Kewl you got a ride in the back of a pickup but oh so dangerous on a highway. Fun ya got to hang with friends out of the storm.

Adventure Links of the Week

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (773 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When we’re not outdoors, we get our adventure fix by exploring social media and the web.
  • Industry observers note that yosemite Visitors Join Forces To Perform Extraordinary Rescue on Half Dome: When a Polish hiker slipped while descending the cables on Yosemite’s Half Dome, she slid down the steep granite face and was left clinging to the rock.
  • Recent findings suggest that A group of strangers came together to rescue the pair.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When we’re not outdoors, we get our adventure fix by exploring social media and the web. Here are some of the best adventure links we’ve discovered this week.

Industry observers note that yosemite Visitors Join Forces To Perform Extraordinary Rescue on Half Dome: When a Polish hiker slipped while descending the cables on Yosemite’s Half Dome, she slid down the steep granite face and was left clinging to the rock. Her fiancé then lost his footing while trying to reach her.

Recent findings suggest that A group of strangers came together to rescue the pair. Using ropes, slings, carabiners, and climbing harnesses, the group formed a human chain to reach both stranded hikers and pull them to safety.

The Electric Arms Race Has Gone Too Far: Tim Shuff questions the growing use of electric motors in outdoor adventure. He argues that the speed and convenience they create undermine traditionally self-propelled activities like paddling and cycling. Today, you can even buy battery-powered SUPs.

While recognizing that electric assistance can make outdoor sports more accessible, he thinks that its wider use will change wilderness areas, reshape trails, and create pressure to build increasingly powerful equipment.

Jan Spicka descends from Huascarán Sur. Photo: Matej Zak.

A Czech Alpinist Describes How He Survived a Nightmare on Peru’s Highest Mountain: Climbing Peru’s Huascarán Sur turned into a tragedy for a group of five friends last July. Czech alpinist Jan Spicka describes how he and partner Matej Zak reached the 6,768m summit before he plunged into a hidden crevasse on the descent.

Matej’s quick reactions saved his life, but their three friends, Saul Mendoza, Chicho Ugarte, and Arti Salas, disappeared while attempting to descend by a different route. With no official mountain rescue in Peru, friends and volunteers pitched in. After 24 hours in the freezing conditions, they knew it was unlikely they would see their friends again. GPS tracks and later searches suggest they had fallen through a collapsing snow bridge.

He Felt Stuck in New York. So He Started Walking to California: Feeling trapped by unemployment and a lack of opportunities in New York, 29-year-old Chantz Rivera began walking across America. He set off with a tent, sleeping bag, and some supplies in a shopping cart. Over 149 days, he walked to California, pushing his cart 32 to 40km a day along highways and through small towns, documenting his progress for his growing number of online followers.

Industry observers note that this Mountain Race Makes Runners Carry 60kg of Beer and Supplies Uphill: Slovakia’s annual Sherpa Rallye is one of the world’s unique mountain races. Competitors have to haul heavy loads of supplies up a 5.7km rocky trail to a remote hut in the High Tatras, nearly 2,000m above sea level.

Men carry 60kg, including a 30-liter keg of beer, while women carry 20kg, with the loads secured to wooden frames. The race was started in 1985 by mountain porter Viktor Beranek. The event brings together the region’s nosiči (traditional mountain porters) and also helps stock the remote hut ahead of winter.

According to recent reports, A Hiker Slid Hundreds of Meters Down Mount Timpanogos: A female hiker was seriously injured after slipping off the trail near the summit of Mount Timpanogos in Utah. She slid several hundred feet down the steep mountainside before landing on a narrow cliff ledge. Newly released helicopter footage reveals her being hoisted to safety. She was taken to hospital and is reportedly recovering.

Recent findings suggest that we Need to Move Past the ‘Shut Up and Die Like a Man’ Mentality in the Mountains: Climber and paraglider Will Gadd reflects on the psychological impact of mountain accidents. Climbing culture often glorifies the dangers people face in the mountains while discouraging them from admitting they are struggling.

Industry observers note that gadd discusses the deaths of two close friends and challenges the underlying expectation that climbers should simply suck it up and carry on. After decades in the mountains, he has seen that the consequences of an accident extend far beyond the immediate incident, affecting survivors and their families and friends for years.

Two Hikers Dead in Bear Attack in British Columbia: Two hikers, identified as 48-year-old Jennifer Balcarras and her 20-year-old daughter Selah Reed, have died in a suspected grizzly attack near the Snooka West Trail in Bella Coola, British Columbia. Their bodies were found during a search after the pair were reported missing by their family.

This comes just a year after a separate grizzly attack in the same area severely injured four people, including three children. The trail remains closed as authorities continue their investigation.

#33087. Antarctica 2026-2027: Expedition Roundup

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (957 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Antarctica 2026-2027: Expedition Roundup

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (957 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here are the Antarctic expeditions for 2026-27.
  • It has been revealed that hercules Inlet is the common starting point for South Pole skiers.
  • According to recent reports, brit Nathan Lumb originally planned a fully unsupported round-trip to the South Pole but scaled back due to “expedition logistics and funding realities.” He will now ski solo and unsupported from Hercules Inlet to the South Pole.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here are the Antarctic expeditions for 2026-27. There will be more, as a few still scramble to raise the money or choose to keep their looks to themselves until the last minute. Because of the long charter flights, an expedition to Antarctica, even a “tourist” Last Degree trip, costs close to $100,000 — more, if you want to do something unusual. These are the journeys declared so far. Skiers hit the ice later this month.

It has been revealed that hercules Inlet is the common starting point for South Pole skiers. Skiers need to travel around 1,130km, averaging around 20km per day.

According to recent reports, brit Nathan Lumb originally planned a fully unsupported round-trip to the South Pole but scaled back due to “expedition logistics and funding realities.” He will now ski solo and unsupported from Hercules Inlet to the South Pole. Lumb previously completed a crossing of Norway’s Finnmarksvidda with guiding company Ousland Colliard.

It has been revealed that indian Neeraj Choudhary also trained with Ousland Colliard, crossing the Greenland Ice Sheet in 2024. He hopes to become the second Indian to ski solo and unsupported to the South Pole, following Satish Gogineni, who became the first in 2024-2025.

Satish Gogineni at the South Pole in 2025. Photo: Satish Gogineni.

Industry observers note that american Lucas Czarnecki will also ski solo and unsupported and claims he will livestream every moment of his journey: “What sets South Signal [his expedition name] apart from other polar expeditions is my commitment to bringing you along for every moment of this extreme adventure. Each day, I will be live-streaming my experience directly from the ice, sharing the raw reality of life on the polar plateau.”.

According to recent reports, another American, Meghan Buchanan, will also tackle the route. She looks to start early, leaving for Antarctica on November 12.

Finally, German Dirk Langer will also attempt the route unsupported.

A Berkner Island start means a few extra kilometers, with skiers required to cover around 1,400km to the South Pole.

Industry observers note that max Worsley of the UK and Martin Nesse of Norway also blueprint to start in early November, but from the edge of Berkner Island. Max is the son of Henry Worsley, who died following an Antarctic expedition in 2015-2016. Max intends to follow much of his father’s final route.

Recent findings suggest that at least two expeditions will begin at the Messner start, 911km from the South Pole. James Garnett of the UK and Norwegian Marius Rehn will each ski solo and unsupported.

Satish Gogineni will be back in Antarctica this year, hoping to build upon his Hercules Inlet experience. Gogineni’s 2026 initiative is more ambitious: a solo, 2,000km journey from the outer edge of the Filchner–Ronne Ice Shelf to the inner edge of the Ross Ice Shelf via the South Pole. Gogineni is billing this as a “world-first human achievement” and the “longest solo traverse ever completed on the Antarctic continent.”.

If successful, his route would indeed be longer than the truncated crossings of Colin O’Brady and Lou Rudd in 2018. However, his distance would still be well short of Borge Ousland’s 1997 expedition. Ousland became the first person to cross Antarctica solo and unsupported, though he occasionally used a rudimentary handheld kite known as a ski sail. Ousland skied for 65 days and covered 2,845km. At the time, sails were not considered “support.”.

Last year, O’Brady tried a significantly longer expedition than his 2018 effort, attempting to ski from the edge of the Ross Ice Shelf to the tip of Berkner Island on the edge of the Ronne Ice Shelf, a total distance of over 2,800km. He eventually ended his crossing attempt after 100 days, with roughly 40% of his total distance remaining.

A map by PECS (the Polar Expeditions Classification Scheme) showing previous solo Antarctic crossing routes. Photo: PECS.

Gogineni’s main challenge might be the weight of his sled. With so much weight spread over two sleds, O’Brady was forced to double carry in soft snow on the Ross Ice Shelf last year. A double carry involved shuttling half of his gear forward, then returning to pick up the rest. This meant he had to cover 15km for every 5km of progress. Gogineni claims his sled will weigh 181kg.

Mardi Philips, Ida Olsson, and Nia Owens are calling themselves the Antarctic Valkyries and aim to become the “first all-female team to reach the South Pole of Inaccessibility.” They will start at Thorshammer Station (a spot near the Russian Novolazarevskaya Station in Queen Maud Land) and plan to kite-ski 2,500km, first aiming for the Pole of Inaccessibility (the middle of the Antarctic continent), and then continuing to their finish point at the South Pole.

Sources indicate that the Antarctic Valkyries proposed route. Photo: Antarctic Valkyries.

A Spanish scientific expedition will cross Antarctica by a fresh route in a unique wind-powered vehicle.

Part of the wind-sled involves a series of tents. Photo: La Vanguardia.

Their “wind-sled ” is 15m long and consists of four modules. It is propelled using 20 kites of various sizes. The largest kite measures 150m² and the smallest 5m². The four-man team prepares a 3,400km, 85-day journey from near Novolazarevskaya Station to the Italian research station Concordia, known as Dome C, on the Antarctic Plateau.

The wind-sled team’s proposed route. The green return route is planned for a future expedition. Photo: La Vanguardia.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, three Argentine kayakers are preparing to paddle roughly 900km along the western coast of the Antarctic Peninsula, from Argentina’s Esperanza Base to San Martín Base. Diego Linares, Juan Tomaselli, and Javier Siede will start their journey in January and strategy to spend 30 to 40 days on the water.

#33083. A Risky Summit Push on Everest

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (626 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

A Risky Summit Push on Everest

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (626 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s now or never for the Russian team on the West Ridge of Everest.
  • In a recent development, everest is still loaded with fresh snow after two cyclones, and there are only three of them to break trail and find the best route above 7,500m.
  • “It looks like we have a weather window of about a week, followed by a significant intensification of the wind,” leader Andrei Vasiliev told Anna Piunova of Mountain Club.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s now or never for the Russian team on the West Ridge of Everest. Andrey Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov have set off for the summit without oxygen, hoping the weather will hold. They are completely alone on the mountain, and the push is full of risk.

In a recent development, everest is still loaded with fresh snow after two cyclones, and there are only three of them to break trail and find the best route above 7,500m. That was their highest point during their earlier venture in October. In addition, the wind may rise dramatically on Thursday, Vitor Baia, a Portuguese high-altitude meteorologist, told ExplorersWeb.

“It looks like we have a weather window of about a week, followed by a significant intensification of the wind,” leader Andrei Vasiliev told Anna Piunova of Mountain Club.

The question is exactly when the wind will increase, and whether the climbers will have enough time to summit and descend to a safer altitude.

“They have three days of weak wind, until Wednesday [November 11], but then the wind will increase sharply,” stated Baia.

He says the best summit day will be Tuesday, with clear skies and weak winds. “Then they could use Wednesday to descend,” he added. “[That day will have] some clouds but still acceptable wind speeds.”.

The situation will worsen remarkably on Thursday, when the wind will shift from the west to the northwest and increase dramatically to 50 kph at 8,000m and 60kph at the summit.

In addition, avalanche hazards are still high due to the large amounts of snow after the latest storm two weeks ago. Finally, as winter approaches, it’s getting colder every day, the climbers reported.

After their first trip up ended in a tactical retreat as the cyclone hit, they retreated to Kathmandu to recover from some health issues. Now they are fit again and ready for a second try. They returned to Base Camp last Thursday. Not surprisingly, they found it covered in a thick fresh layer of snow. Breaking trail, they sank at some points up to their waists, Vasiliev reported.

According to recent reports, “Our high-altitude boots were in a cache two hours ahead of us, so we used duct tape to seal our pant cuffs to our trekking boots, trying to keep the snow out,” Kondrashkin reported. They eventually reached the cache and continued up in an exhausting 14-hour-long effort to a second cache (their Camp 1), where they had left their tent and sleeping bags.

They were near an avalanche-prone area and several snow slides swept nearby, prompting them to wait a day before continuing. Meanwhile, Shipilov demonstrated signs of food poisoning. Kodrashkin recalls that Saturday morning started with the following conversation:.

I wake up at 4:00 to boil some water.

“Vitalya, how are you feeling? Are we heading up?”.

That answer needs some clarification. A professional like Vitaly Viktorovich [Shipilov] really only has two modes: “We’re going” and “I’m dying.”.

In fact, Shipilov had a fever and acute pain in the lower back, so the team headed down to their base in Lobuche. As this was going on, the snow had time to sluff off from the previously avalanche-prone area.

After just one night of rest, Vasiliev confirmed they were going up again. If all went according to blueprint, they will spend tonight back in their tent above the Lho La. Unfortunately, the climbers have not shared their tracker showing their current location and progress. On their previous trip up, they reached some 7,500m on Everest’s West Shoulder, near the beginning of the West Ridge and the potential detour to the Hornbein Couloir.

It has been revealed that everest’s North Face from the base of the West Ridge. Photo: Sergey Kondrashkin.

Breaking: Winners of the Banff Mountain Film Festival Declared

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (792 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The annual Banff Centre Mountain Festival gathers mountain luminaries from across the world at the Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity in Alberta.
  • Sources indicate that the Grand Prize went to Listen, directed by Taliesin Black-Brown.
  • Rose Bush, an Oscar Award-winning director of photography serving on the competition’s jury, called Listen “a film that engages human-caused environmental devastation — the existential dilemma of our time — at its nucleus with overwhelming love and hope.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The annual Banff Centre Mountain Festival gathers mountain luminaries from across the world at the Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity in Alberta. There, a celebration of mountain culture recognizes the best outdoor films and books of the past year. The climax of the festival took place this past weekend, and the winners of the 51st annual Banff Mountain Film Competition have now been announced.

Sources indicate that the Grand Prize went to Listen, directed by Taliesin Black-Brown. In this short documentary, sound engineer Hank Lentfer records the sounds of nature around his Alaska home, while caring for his mother with dementia. As Lentfer documents the degradation of the natural world, we witness the slow loss of his mother. Drawing together these two threads, the film explores connection despite, and through, loss, using sound.

Rose Bush, an Oscar Award-winning director of photography serving on the competition’s jury, called Listen “a film that engages human-caused environmental devastation — the existential dilemma of our time — at its nucleus with overwhelming love and hope.”.

The film also won the Grand Jury Prize at the Tribeca Film Festival.

In addition to a grand prize, the festival honors films in several categories. The winning film in the Adventure category was The Navigator, a feature-length work from director Jordan Manley. The film follows Nainoa Thompson, who was the first Native Hawaiian in six centuries to make the journey from Hawaii to Tahiti in a traditional voyaging canoe. Now, almost five decades later, Thompson and his crew make the journey again, using only traditional navigation techniques.

It has been revealed that the best film in the Mountain Culture category was Land of Canaan, produced and directed by Maggie Lemere. Lemere’s film follows a group of Palestinian olive farmers, who work to protect their ancient olive groves amid the destruction by Israel. The film “illuminated the vital relationship of courage, vision, hope, and traditional ecological knowledge,” juror Rose Bush said, “in service of the essential value of sovereignty via mountain culture.”.

In the Environment category, director James Dawson’s winning comedic documentary Derek vs Derek follows two Devon farmers, both named Derek. One Derek is an ardent dairy farmer while his environmentalist neighbor begins rewilding his land. A feud naturally ensues.

Industry observers note that the Arc’teryx-sponsored Best Climbing Film was Zindabad, directed by Tom Fish. Fish follows Pakistani climber Mueez Ud Din into the Karakoram, alongside his uncle Javed Ali and French climber Mathieu Maynadier. Ud Din explores a remote, unknown glacier system, while the film examines what it means to be a Pakistani climber among peaks long claimed by international outsiders.

Directed by Alexis Berg, the Mountain Sports winner, Roots, follows trail runner Ruth Croft as she examines her future as an elite ultra-trail runner after an injury. Roots is “about an inner journey of healing and acceptance, rooted in the essential joy of running outdoors,” explained juror David Arnaud.

Sources indicate that the Snow Sports winner centers on American skier Jessie Diggins. Diggins is the most decorated American cross-country skier ever, but Threshold, directed by Torsten Brinkema, reveals the deep personal struggles behind that success. Juror Beki Henderson noted that “the jury particularly commends Jessie Diggins for her extraordinary courage and honesty in sharing her story.”.

Industry observers note that there were more mountain films this year than you can even imagine. With 610 film submissions and 83 finalists, it’s no wonder that there are still more category winners.

Best short film winner Hello, Beautiful follows climber Alannah Yip as she struggles with identity, training for the Olympics while enduring medical hair loss. Director Darcy Hennessey created a film which “reminds us that personal transformation does not always come from pushing harder,” juror Kerry Stauffer explained.

For best feature film, the competition unveiled Ceremony, directed and produced by Banchi Hanuse. The film tells the story of the disappearance of the ooligan, a small fish, from British Columbia’s Bella Coola River. Jurors praised the film’s use of watercolor animation, personal stories, and community broadcasts to explore the importance of a seemingly unimportant little fish.

According to recent reports, director Marco Tribelhorn’s 75 seconds won the Creative Excellence Award. The film documents free-skier Jacob Wester’s 75-second-long battle for survival while trapped in an avalanche.

“A compelling visual treatment brings to life an experience that is impossible to imagine,” said Kerry Stauffer.

It has been revealed that last but not least, the Audience Choice Award went to Only Music // Snake River. Director Justin Fountain’s documentary follows a band that ditches the tour bus for a journey down the Snake River, seeking connection with strangers.

Tickets for the international film festival are now available. We have also covered the recently unveiled Banff Mountain Book Award winners.

Te Araroa: Food abominations and creations from the first weeks on trail

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (699 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This was Sven’s invention, the first one he let me try was made in a garlic flavoured wrap.
  • A concoction involving a rotating seasoning sachet du jour (this day it was carbonara) mixed in with a packet of tuna and some pasta.
  • This was my invention at the Puhoi tea rooms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This was Sven’s invention, the first one he let me try was made in a garlic flavoured wrap. I’m sorry to say that it was delicious and I ended up eating peanut butter cheese wraps for the next week of lunches. You do have to eat this with some candy or something high in sugar otherwise you’ll find yourself halfway up a major hill wanting to throw up because your body has been unable to process the fat in the cheese and peanut butter and you will have run out of energy. Or if you’re lucky you’ve just been through a town and can have a side of fresh fruit and vege.

The best blueberries I’ve ever had.

A concoction involving a rotating seasoning sachet du jour (this day it was carbonara) mixed in with a packet of tuna and some pasta. Honestly, once it was all mixed together it didn’t look bad at all. He claims he hasn’t gotten tired of it yet. He has it with a side of vanilla protein. This day he did forget to let the pasta soak so it was a little crunchy.

This was my invention at the Puhoi tea rooms. To be honest I didn’t think it was weird or heinous but literally everyone else did. I’d say I was the real winner here because Sinèad ended up ordering the same thing after me, and guess what?? It was GOOD. The man at the tea room called me weird about six times but still brought me my bacon and it only cost $12 total.

Bacon not pictured because he wouldn’t bring it out at the same time as the scones.

What was I supposed to do, NOT order bacon?

It has been revealed that mash, dehydrated peas, beef jerky and polenta. Mash, peas, TVP. Polenta, instant noodles, peanut butter. Just bits and pieces from various ziploc bags with boiled water and a stock cube and some salt. Again, this is my formula. And I love it. Your goo your way. Delicious. It just looks like nothing anyone would eat in normal life.

When you don’t feel like figuring out what to eat and you only have scraps left in your food bag so you shove a packet of beef jerky in a wrap and call it a day.

This night we hit a supermarket and all good over-zealous in the produce section. The result was an extremely filling but unfortunately low calorie dinner of hot chips and salad in wraps. My body was so happy to eat all the vegetables so it was worth the need to eat extra the next day.

Once in a while you’re blessed with knowledge of something you didn’t know you even needed to know. That’s how felt when I learned about single serve sachets of pizza sauce. So naturally I bought chorizo and Parmesan and ate trail pizzas for lunch for the next several days.

Not much to say about this one other than it SLAPS and you can swap out your yogurt flavours and your oat flavours to keep this fresh. Best consumed in your tent while packing. It also doesn’t look that nice and some days you don’t nail the amount of water so you end up with a drink instead of actual oats. Oh well!!!

A 3,300Km Walk Across Japan in Winter

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (472 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Japanese publisher Katsunari Tanaka has set himself the challenge of hauling a handcart 3,345km from Japan’s northernmost tip to the southern edge of Okinawa in winter.
  • According to recent reports, tanaka, 49, set off from Cape Sōya in Hokkaido on October 7 and is heading south to Cape Hedo in Okinawa.
  • Rather than carrying everything on his back, he is pulling a handcart that weighs around 100kg.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Japanese publisher Katsunari Tanaka has set himself the challenge of hauling a handcart 3,345km from Japan’s northernmost tip to the southern edge of Okinawa in winter.

According to recent reports, tanaka, 49, set off from Cape Sōya in Hokkaido on October 7 and is heading south to Cape Hedo in Okinawa. He hopes to complete the traverse in 100 days over five months. As he will have to contend with some challenging winter conditions along the way, he has described it as “playing chase with winter.”.

Rather than carrying everything on his back, he is pulling a handcart that weighs around 100kg. He also has a support team with a vehicle in case of emergencies. At some points, different members of his team have walked with him for a day or so. His daily target is around 35km, with rest days and organized stops built into the schedule.

The first few weeks have already brought strong headwinds, rain, and some steep climbs, making progress difficult at times. Temperatures have dropped close to freezing. At the end of October, he crossed a mountain pass between Yoichi and Iwanai. There, headwinds stirred up the gravel as he walked. Then the snow began. In the end, he took refuge with his support team until the weather improved.

Sources indicate that despite the conditions, Tanaka reached Hakodate Harbor on November 3, having covered 621km across Hokkaido. From Hakodate, he is crossing the Tsugaru Strait by ferry to Aomori, then will continue south along the Sanriku coast to Sendai.

From there, he follows the Pacific coast through Fukushima to Tokyo before joining the Tokaido route toward Osaka before heading west to Kyushu. A second ferry crossing brings him to Okinawa, where he will walk to his final destination, Cape Hedo.

Sources indicate that along a road in Hokkaido. Photo: Katsunari Tanaka/Instagram.

This is not Tanaka’s first experience of traveling Japan with a handcart. Around a decade ago, he spent three years visiting all 47 prefectures, selling books directly to people he met along the way. Loading his publications onto a cart, he covered the country between 2013 and 2016, eventually selling 13,477 books. At the time, many people questioned what he was doing and whether books could really be sold on the street. But he says the experience shaped his approach to business and his belief in the power of personal connections.

Tanaka insists that he is not an adventurer. Instead, he is traveling the country as a “merchant.” This time, he is making the journey to support his mentor, Arthur Hollands, a Japanese evangelist known for undertaking lengthy walks while carrying a large wooden cross. Along the route, Tanaka prepares to stop at 11 locations to give lectures. He welcomes people to join him for sections of the walk.

Photo: Katsunari Tanaka/Instagram.

#33072. First Ski Descent of Meru Central

First Ski Descent of Meru Central

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (412 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that tiphaine Duperier and Boris Langenstein of France have notched another Himalayan first ski descent, this time down the southwest face of Meru Central (6,310m) in India’s Garhwal Himalaya.
  • Duperier admitted they started the expedition with low expectations after several projects earlier in the fall all failed.
  • “Snow conditions had been unforgiving,” she wrote.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that tiphaine Duperier and Boris Langenstein of France have notched another Himalayan first ski descent, this time down the southwest face of Meru Central (6,310m) in India’s Garhwal Himalaya. The skiers are still surprised by how lucky they were.

Duperier admitted they started the expedition with low expectations after several projects earlier in the fall all failed.

“Snow conditions had been unforgiving,” she wrote. “We figured there was only a 3-in-10 chance of skiing the southwest face of Meru.”.

But when they got there, the mountain was, they added, “generous” with them.

Industry observers note that the three-peaked Meru massif, located in the Gangotri Glacier region of the Garhwal Himalaya, lies between Shivling and Thalay Sagar. It has three peaks: 6,660m Meru South, 6,310m Meru Central, and 6,450m Meru North. The ski descent line is in purple. Photo: Duperier/Langenstein.

“We spent six days of reconnaissance and three [days] climbing the peak, [thanks to] an unprecedented stroke of luck in finding a way through the icefall and perfect snow in the upper section,” she explained.

In a recent development, the icefall on Meru Central. Photo: Boris Langenstein.

Recent findings suggest that the icefall at the base of the peak was indeed one of the most complex passages. The pair climbed a 15m pitch of WI4 and left a safety rope, which they also used to rappel down after the ski descent, Duperier told PlanetMountain.

Otherwise, the pair of regular expedition and skiing partners climbed alpine-style and pretty fast, reaching the summit in less than eight hours. According to their research, they completed the second-ever ascent of the southwest face of Meru, after an Indian team in 2023.

At the summit on Meru Central. Photo: Duperier/Langenstein.

Industry observers note that the skiers estimate they covered 1,500m on their descent, with some sections reaching 50 °. Snow conditions were good overall, hard but with a good grip.

“We skied like little monkeys on the wires in Rishikesh,” Duperier posted on social media. “It was just incredible, truly beautiful!”.

While the climbers rappelled down the icefall onto the glacier below, the ski descent itself had no rappels or interruptions.

Duperier barely had time to return home to France to pick up a Piolet d’Or for the first alpine-style ascent of the Schell Route on the Rupal Face of Nanga Parbat, followed by the first ski descent from the 8,125m summit.

Tiphaine Duperier at the Piolets d’Or ceremony. Photo: Piotr Drozdz.

Arctic Town Kills Dozens of Grizzlies Feeding on Dump

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (322 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For years, the grizzlies near Inuvik in Canada’s western Arctic relied on a stable source of food — the town dump.
  • In 2025, before the fence was built, trail cameras captured multiple grizzlies hanging around the dump, looking for food.
  • Recent findings suggest that it was too much.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For years, the grizzlies near Inuvik in Canada’s western Arctic relied on a stable source of food — the town dump. Generations of bears grew up feeding there. In 2025, wildlife officials found that over 40 grizzlies regularly visited the dump.

In 2025, before the fence was built, trail cameras captured multiple grizzlies hanging around the dump, looking for food. Photo: Government of the Northwest Territories.

Recent findings suggest that it was too much. This year, the town built an electric fence around the site, hoping the bears would move on. They didn’t. Some started coming into town looking for food. Others just hung around the fence, searching for a way in.

According to recent reports, “They would just do these laps around the dump, and they would just be emaciated, sickly,” mentioned Toby Halle, a Renewable Resources officer based in Inuvik, told the CBC. “They don’t know what to do with themselves. And quite frankly, we don’t know what to do with them.”.

In a recent development, inuvik, population about 3,500, was the first community in that part of the Arctic to try to wean the bears off their dependence on dump food with such a fence, which cost about $700,000. The problem was, the bears had not learned to depend on any other source of food.

It has been revealed that “We’ve probably had three to four generations of bears that have been using that landfill,” mentioned local mayor Peter Clarkson. In the end, the town took a drastic solution — but one that was probably unavoidable in the circumstances: They shot 28 bears.

Tragic though this is, officials hope that within the next couple of years, the remaining bears in the area will move on and learn to eat more natural fare.

Recent findings suggest that many other Arctic towns still have open dumps where bears come to feed. Photo: Government of the Northwest Territories.

#33065. Red’s Meadow Via Rabid Coyote — John Muir Trail Day 19

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2955 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Red’s Meadow Via Rabid Coyote — John Muir Trail Day 19

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2955 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The previous night I spoke with my wife Lee.
  • Sources indicate that on this occasion she asked me what I was thinking and feeling about the rupture with my sisters.
  • It has been revealed that it was actually great to have that knoll above the trail all to myself.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Total Elevation Gain: 40,482  feet.

Pace (minutes per mile):  22:41.

The previous night I spoke with my wife Lee. I will admit to a little ambivalence. On the one hand, of course it was great to hear her voice and learn what was happening in the outside world. On the other hand, the usual lack of communication (except for very short Garmin texts) is a kind of shelter from the problems and worries of that outside world. It means you can really just focus on putting one foot in front of the other in your thru-hike bubble.

Sources indicate that on this occasion she asked me what I was thinking and feeling about the rupture with my sisters. The honest answer was that it had not been in the front of my mind. Her raising it, however, pushed it back into my consciousness in a way that led to a more restless night. This was not necessarily a bad thing. I had some insights that were useful for going forward. But it did mean my sleep was not as restful as it might have been, waking in the middle of the night as the bright, bright moon shone down.

It has been revealed that it was actually great to have that knoll above the trail all to myself. For a reason I do not understand, I was a little bit paranoid about bears, so I was extra careful to keep my bear cannister well away from my tent. As far as I know, no bears visited in the night.

According to recent reports, in the morning, the light began to shine, but it was cold, so I just stayed in my sleeping bag, rehearsing the lines for the play I was cast in. I knew Red’s Meadow was not far, and I could easily make it there well in advance of lunch, even if I had a lazy morning. Eventually I did get up and did all those things that I do in the morning.

Sources indicate that tent stowed and pack packed. If you look carefully, you can see the trail down below, beyond the boulder.

It has been revealed that ninja Queen told me about her practice of putting on hiking clothes first thing and I have adopted it. It links to the technique I already used of stuffing my sleeping bag in its sack right away, to ensure that I’m not tempted to go back inside it. I call these motivational tricks “outsmarting my own stupidity.”.

After breakfast it started to warm up a bit, I finished packing, and I hit the road.

Sources indicate that the night before, when I considered a 4-5 mile night hike to Red’s Meadow Resort, I worried in case the trail was difficult or dangerous to navigate in the darkness. In the daylight it was actually a very cruisy trail.

So, I need not have worried, though there was at least one stream-crossing bridge that left a little to be desired!

Despite the damage, this was still the best option for crossing this little stream!

In addition, at night I would have missed the red cones. I had seen that marking on the map and wondered if it referred to a forest whose trees produce red pine cones. On the contrary, they were two red cinder cones, a testament to the recent volcanic activity in this area. Geologically, they were extremely recent, having erupted less than 10,000 years ago. Seeing them left me with the question, “What gives lava or cinders or basaltic rock a reddish color, as opposed to the black color, which we more usually associate with vulcanism?”.

I got no answer then, but now AI tells me:.

Basaltic lavas are rich in iron and magnesium. When this iron-rich material is exposed to oxygen and water vapor—either while erupting into the air, interacting with steam, or weathering over time—the iron oxidizes and forms iron oxide minerals (such as hematite), turning the rock red, orange, or rust-brown.

By contrast, the classic black color of fresh basalt and volcanic glass (obsidian) happens when iron- and magnesium-bearing minerals cool quickly with limited oxygen exposure, or while the rock is still in its dense, un-oxidized state.

Recent findings suggest that most of the trail was downhill, so I was making fast time even without pushing it. It went down steadily, but not steeply.

View toward rocky crags across the valley.

Two male southbound hikers slowed as they approached me and gestured me to stop. They noted, “You should know there’s been a coyote behaving very oddly down at the river where you are headed. It was unafraid of people, it was out in the open during the daytime, and it seemed to be hanging around for no apparent purpose. We banged our hiking poles together but that did not chase it away. It was acting very strangely.”.

I replied, “Well, I am not afraid of coyotes, but I’m very afraid of the virus that may be in that coyote’s saliva, because it sounds like it may be rabid.”.

I put a rock in my pocket, “just in case,” and continued on.

Shortly, another couple came up the trail, and I asked them whether they had seen anything.

According to recent reports, “Oh, we think we saw a fox,” the guy stated and he pulled out his phone to show me a picture. It was definitely a coyote, but I could tell they were Europeans, and surely didn’t know what a coyote was. It was concerning that it was close enough and tame enough that they could take a picture of it so readily.

Industry observers note that dropping down further, the trail broke out of the forest into a large area where there must have been a significant forest fire. There were a large number of standing dead trees and a certain amount of underbrush, a sort of desert chaparral kind of vegetation.

Neither the first, nor the last, fire-damaged landscape.

Sources indicate that notable was a bushy shrub that was putting out thick clusters of small, dark ash-blue berries. I did not know what they were, but I  was not about to eat a few berries to find out!

Sources indicate that do leave me a comment if you know what these berries are! (I suspect Blue Elderberry, Sambucus Cerulea).

In this exposed terrain I encountered yet another couple, two women this time, who also reported seeing this coyote, and saying how seemingly tame it was. I remarked, “He didn’t lick you, or, or put any saliva on you, did he?”.

They assured me that had not happened, and I was relieved. They also told me the coyote was at the river crossing, where I would not be going as I was about to turn right off the trail to go to Red’s Meadow. That was a relief, as a rabid coyote worried me a lot more than a healthy bear!

Sources indicate that these women also seemed better informed about the weather report, and that news was not good. They said, “It looks like this afternoon there’s going to be rain, becoming very steady and maybe even heavy tonight. Then tomorrow, all day long, there’s a danger of lightning and thunderstorms, possibly severe.”  Yikes!

Sources indicate that that sounded a bit ominous. Now, I don’t mind being in a tent when it’s raining. In fact, it can be a little bit cozy to be dry and warm while the rain patters on the rain fly above you.

The next morning, however, is different. Having to pack up when everything is muddy, and the tent is wet? That I do not enjoy at all! That’s a major headache, because what do you do? Do you wait until the sun comes out later in the day, to dry everything out? Or do you just slog on carrying your wet tent? Especially with the next day’s forecast being so ominous, spending the night tenting in the rain was unattractive.

Recent findings suggest that then I remembered that I had cell service the night before. I thought, “Maybe I can find the phone number for Red’s Meadow and make a booking?”  So, I looked it up and called them from the trail.

Industry observers note that london answered. No, not England, that was just the name of the young woman I spoke to. She looked it up and reported they still had lodging for that night. She stated the PCT Cabin was available and would be the best deal for a single hiker. I was set!

After further descent, I saw the sign marking the turn off from the main stem of the John Muir Trail. I was almost there.

The first thing I saw was a sort of livestock area, and then there was a signpost that indicated the distance in miles to Canada, Mexico, the Devil’s Postpile, and many other places, near and far. The arrow pointing to Red’s Meadow store was ambiguous, however, and I read it to indicate a path that goes down to a lower parking area.

According to recent reports, after a descent of 100 feet or so, I found more signage in the lower parking lot. This time it showed Red’s Meadow Resort to be up a black, brand latest, paved tar road, pointing right back in the direction from which I had just come. So, I huffed and puffed back up the hill and turned left into Red’s Meadow. I must admit, the sign had seen better days (see the featured image above).

Recent findings suggest that it is interesting how expectations get set. I went first to the Muir Trail Ranch with no expectations, and I took that as the resupply stop norm. Then I went to Vermilion Valley Resort, and I reset that as the fresh norm. Now, in Red’s Meadow, it dawned on me that there is no “norm.”  Each is its own separate thing, different and unique.

Sources indicate that I found London in the store and paid her the $179 for a night in the cabin. It was oddly intermediate between the $375 I paid at MTR and the $25 I paid at VVR. The cabin was not ready yet because they were cleaning it, so I dropped my pack under an awning by the restaurant and explored the place.

There was a sort of central area with picnic tables. Around it the store was on one side, and the restaurant on the other. In the surrounding area, there were three stalls for men’s showers, ditto for women’s, and a laundry in between. Separately, there were latrines for men and women. The lodging (or at least mine) was just outside this central area.

View across the picnic tables towards the restaurant at Red’s Meadow.

As I wandered around, I discovered that Ninja Queen was there!

The Queen, in full Ninja regalia!

I thought she was planning to overnight, but she had a very specific date targeted to complete the trail, and was worried about missing that mark. For that reason, she had picked up her resupply but had packed it up right away. Now she was shouldering a much heavier pack and continuing on her way. In no time she was gone.

According to recent reports, I realized that I probably would never see her again. I had her phone number and email, however, for sending photos taken on the trail.

Recent findings suggest that idly wandering, I went in the store, hoping there might be some boot socks, because mine were getting ever-larger holes in them. There were none. What they did have was a good selection of beer at a very reasonable price. I got a local brew to drink later.

Industry observers note that outside the rain was coming in occasional drips, a harbinger of a storm moving in. When the restaurant opened at noon, I was first in line. Lunch was a double cheeseburger with a huge chocolate milkshake, and a nice little bowl of potato salad. The shake was perfect; the rest was fine.

After lunch, I was given the keys to my cabin. It was clean and appeared well constructed. It had a small settee and a bunk bed and electricity to charge electronics. At half the price it was still a nicer space than MTR.

It has been revealed that I wore my rain poncho while I did my laundry. This allowed me to wash everything. Of course, within three hours on the trail, it’ll be as dirty as if I’d never used the laundry at all; but for those three hours, it will feel blissful. I took a shower but did not even touch the rat’s nest that was once my ponytail.

It has been revealed that afterwards I did a little more grooming. I trimmed my mustache, so it is not dragging in my food. Most important, I cut my nails and filed them with an emery board so there are no jagged, loose edges. The toenails are key, because hiking with long toenails can lead to all sorts of problems, especially a subungual hematoma, also known as “black toe.”.

If you can help it, you don’t want THAT!

In a recent development, my only real criticism of Red’s Meadow is that they are open for both lunch and dinner from 12 to 6 p.m. I had lunch right at 12:15 and then I went for dinner at 5:30, so that I wasn’t ordering the second before they closed. But that’s not normally a wide enough window for two meals. Fortunately, with hiker hunger, it was manageable. I had a tuna melt because I had eaten enough hamburger, and then I had another ginormous milkshake, because you can never have enough chocolate milkshake.

It has been revealed that back in the cabin, I drank my local brew. It was a Yosemite pale ale, produced by the Mammoth Brewing Company from Mammoth Lakes, California. Mammoth is accessible by bus from Red’s Meadow, and significant buses arrive and leave several times a day, but I was not tempted to explore town life.

After laundry, it looks so nice all folded!

I spoke to son Ben and found out some great news: his student loan was canceled, and he was loving his new job. Less great was that the next day he would start the second session of his new chemotherapy. He was getting infusions at the hospital every two weeks as he battled his recurrence of colon cancer.

In a recent development, with time to spare, I learned another page of my part in the play “Almost, Maine” that I will begin rehearsing when I get off trail. I thought learning it on trail would be easy, but most days I have been too tired to give it much attention. This Nero (“Near Zero”) Day gave me some room to do that.

I also unpacked my resupply bucket and separated what I needed from what I wanted to leave behind. I would add to their free hiker’s bucket in the morning as I headed out.

Recent findings suggest that looking ahead, I realized that the end of the trail was not so far off. Red’s Meadow was my last resupply after all. The next two days would include some serious elevation gain, culminating in my entering Yosemite when I cross Donahue Pass. I hoped the residual milkshake effect would power me through! After that, I had two or three long mileage days to the end in Happy Isles, but the elevation change would be mostly downhill. The only wild card was the possibility of getting a permit to climb the Half Dome in Yosemite.

According to recent reports, the horse (me!) was starting to sniff the barn a little bit. I hoped to stay healthy for the next several days. When people on the trail asked me whether I was hiking the whole John Muir Trail, I always answered, “I am trying to.”  Maybe it was superstition, but I never wanted to assume success before achieving it. Even on the very last day on trail, that would be my answer.

According to recent reports, as I prepared for bed, the sound of the raindrops on the roof reminded me that the next day might be wet. It was also disappointing because, on this night of all nights, a total lunar eclipse would occur. On a clear night I would have made looks to check it out. On this night that was hopeless.

Instead, I snuggled in my nice dry cabin and fell asleep.
